procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 05.08.2014 passed by the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in CRLA No. 1136 of 2013, as well as the judgment and order dated 17th May 2013 passed by the trial court.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: All three accused preferred appeals before the High Court. The High Court dismissed all their appeals via judgment and order dated 5th August 2014. Specifically mentioned are Criminal Appeal Nos. 1242, 936 and 1136 of 2013.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Leave was granted in appeal arising out of SLP(Crl.) No. 6213 of 2021. The Supreme Court heard the appeal and allowed it, quashing the judgments of both the High Court and the Trial Court.

decision.conviction_status: acquitted of all the charges levelled against them
directions: They are directed to be set at liberty if not required in any other case.
Bail bonds of the appellants shall stand discharged.

issue.issue_text: In a prosecution case where father was found dead by the complainant-brother of the deceased, and suspicion arose on the son of the deceased on account of the property dispute between the father and the son, and the son ﬂ ed from the scene of incident and was apprehended two days later, whether the courts below were justiﬁ ed in convicting the son u/s. 302/34 IPC and sentencing him to rigorous imprisonment for life.

facts: A father was found dead, and his brother (the complainant) filed a report.
Suspicion was cast upon the deceased's son due to an ongoing property dispute between them.
The prosecution alleged that the son had previously beaten and threatened to kill his father.
The son fled the scene of the incident and was apprehended two days later.
The trial court and the High Court convicted the son for murder under Section 302/34 of the IPC based on this circumstantial evidence.
law: The case was based entirely on circumstantial evidence.
For a conviction based on circumstantial evidence, the prosecution must establish a complete and unbroken chain of circumstances that points only to the guilt of the accused.
The prosecution must prove all incriminating circumstances beyond a reasonable doubt.
Suspicion, no matter how strong, cannot take the place of proof beyond a reasonable doubt.
application: The Supreme Court found that the prosecution "utterly failed" to prove the case and establish the required chain of incriminating circumstances.
The Court evaluated the key pieces of evidence presented by the prosecution and found them to be weak and unreliable.
Specifically, the evidence related to the "last seen theory" was deemed "totally unreliable."
The evidence from the Call Detail Records (CDRs) did not "inspire any confidence."
The Court also found the test identification parade to be of "doubtful" sanctity because the accused had already been shown to the witnesses at the police station.
With the primary pieces of circumstantial evidence failing, the motive (property dispute) and the act of fleeing were reduced to mere suspicion, which is insufficient for a conviction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the lower courts' decisions, holding that the conviction was unjustified. The prosecution failed to prove the incriminating circumstances beyond a reasonable doubt, and its case was based on unreliable evidence and strong suspicion, which cannot substitute for legal proof. Therefore, the Court quashed the conviction and acquitted the son.

arguments.issue_text: In a prosecution case where father was found dead by the complainant-brother of the deceased, and suspicion arose on the son of the deceased on account of the property dispute between the father and the son, and the son ﬂ ed from the scene of incident and was apprehended two days later, whether the courts below were justiﬁ ed in convicting the son u/s. 302/34 IPC and sentencing him to rigorous imprisonment for life.
appellant_arguments: The case is based on circumstantial evidence, and a conviction is not permissible unless the prosecution establishes an unbroken link of circumstances.
respondent_arguments: The High Court and the trial court concurrently convicted the appellants on a proper appreciation of evidence, and therefore, no interference is warranted.

cases.case_name: Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: Circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established and the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Suspicion, however strong, cannot take the place of proof beyond a reasonable doubt. In cases based on circumstantial evidence, the following conditions must be met: the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is drawn must be fully established ('must or should be proved', not 'may be proved'); the established facts must be consistent only with the hypothesis of the accused's guilt and not explainable by any other hypothesis; the circumstances must be of a conclusive nature, excluding every possible hypothesis except the one to be proved; and there must be a complete chain of evidence that leaves no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with the accused's innocence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court found that the prosecution's case, being based on circumstantial evidence, failed to meet the stringent standard of proof required for a conviction. The prosecution did not establish an unbroken chain of circumstances that pointed exclusively to the guilt of the accused. Specifically, the Court deemed the evidence related to the 'last seen' theory to be totally unreliable and the evidence from Call Detail Records (CDRs) to be uninspiring of any confidence, leading to the conclusion that the prosecution had utterly failed to prove the incriminating circumstances beyond a reasonable doubt.
legal_tests_applied: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the following conditions must be fulfilled: (1) the circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be fully established; (2) the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused, that is to say, they should not be explainable on any other hypothesis except that the accused is guilty; (3) the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency; (4) they should exclude every possible hypothesis except the one sought to be proved; and (5) there must be a chain of evidence so complete as not to leave any reasonable ground for the conclusion consistent with the innocence of the accused and must show that in all human probability the act must have been done by the accused.
The circumstances concerned “must or should” and not “may be” established, as there is a legal distinction between “may be proved” and “must be or should be proved”.
However strong a suspicion may be, it cannot take the place of a proof beyond reasonable doubt.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution utterly failed to prove the case as they need to prove the incriminating circumstances beyond reasonable doubt.
The evidence with regard to the last seen theory was found to be totally unreliable.
The evidence regarding the Call Detail Records (CDRs) was one which does not inspire any confidence.
